title: Microsoft Teams
subtitle: People call my digital employee in Teams and it answers; they invite it to meetings and it presents, shares a screen and calls on raised hands. It does not raise its own, because the platform offers no way to.

stats.label: meeting actions with exact schemas, each naming the acting employee
Teams media soak from Azure to Linux
receive stalls through the soak and a forced mid-call reconnect

lede: Helix exists because I wanted one AI colleague that shows up where people already work, under an identity the organisation governs, and behaves in a call and a meeting the way a colleague does. People call the digital employee in Teams and it answers. Call audio crosses from a .NET 8 service on the Microsoft real-time media SDK to a Rust voice engine on my GPUs. When someone talks over the agent, it stops. A Teams call is one more implementation of the engine's sealed audio interface, so the same conversation engine runs on a desk microphone and in Teams. See A self-hosted colleague in a Teams call.
quote: Reporting a hand as raised from local state would be a lie nobody in the meeting could see through.
evidence: Microsoft Teams real-time media: a self-hosted AI participant whose Rust voice engine treats a Teams call as one more implementation of its sealed audio interface, with a 30 min soak and 0 receive stalls.
AI agents in Microsoft Teams meetings: 13 meeting actions with exact schemas, each naming the acting employee, each counted done only when it works in a real meeting.
Teams app development: a meeting-stage app on TeamsJS with an authenticated relay so the agent drives a deck, and a React personal tab signed in through Teams single sign-on with MSAL and PKCE.
Screen-sharing pipelines: a headless Linux desktop captured with FFmpeg and framed as H.264 under one typed frame contract across Linux, Windows and Teams.
author: Corey James
